beginner.headline: Alison Hammond's Live TV Health Scare
beginner.brief: Alison Hammond feared she was having a heart attack on live TV. She went to the hospital for a heart check-up. But it was a panic attack, not a heart attack. She said, "I couldn't catch my breath and I genuinely thought I was having a heart attack." Panic attacks can happen to anyone. A panic attack can feel like a heart attack because symptoms are similar. You can try to calm yourself by breathing slowly.

intermediate.headline: Alison Hammond's Health Scare: Panic Attack on Live TV
intermediate.brief: TV presenter Alison Hammond experienced a health scare during a live broadcast last week. She quickly left the programme, clutching her chest, and went to the hospital for a check-up. Doctors confirmed she had suffered a panic attack, not a heart attack, which she described as "probably one of the most scariest things I've ever been through". Hammond explained she couldn't catch her breath and genuinely believed she was having a heart attack on air. She added that the experience felt very real, like "a wave" of adrenaline overwhelming her body. Upon returning to her weekly slot, she expressed gratitude, saying the event had given her a new perspective on life. She even compared the feeling to entering a place, like the "Upside Down world" from the TV show Stranger Things. She admitted she was anxious about returning to the show, fearing that if she didn't come back immediately, she might never do so. Panic attacks are an extreme anxiety response that can cause both physical and mental symptoms. These attacks can mimic heart attack symptoms such as chest pain, but heart attack pain often spreads to the arm or jaw. To manage a panic attack, experts advise focusing on the present moment, one's surroundings, and steadying one's breathing.

advanced.headline: Alison Hammond's On-Air Health Scare: A Panic Attack Experience
advanced.brief: Television presenter Alison Hammond recounted her alarming experience of feeling as though she was having a cardiac event while live on ITV's This Morning last week. She left the programme midway through the broadcast, visibly clutching her chest before being hospitalised for a medical assessment. She later discovered she had suffered a panic attack, an experience she described as one of the 'scariest things I've ever been through'. Returning to her weekly slot, Hammond explained she couldn't catch her breath, genuinely thought she was having a heart attack, and expressed immense gratitude for being present. She added that the physical sensation felt "very real" and exactly "like a heart attack". Hammond described the instantaneous onset of the panic attack as a sudden wave of adrenaline that overwhelmed her body. Overwhelmed by the sensation, she immediately ran off the set, something she stated she would never normally do on live television. This frightening episode has instigated a profound shift in her outlook, prompting her to re-evaluate life and prioritise her well-being. She likened the surreal feeling of the attack to entering the 'Upside Down world' from the television series Stranger Things. Despite initial apprehension, she deemed it crucial to return to work quickly, thereby avoiding associating the panic with the programme itself. She engaged in discussions with Williams regarding the demanding pressures of presenting live television. Dr Williams clarified that while panic attacks and heart attacks share some symptoms, they are distinct medical conditions. She explained that heart attack pain typically radiates to areas like the arm or jaw, and does not subside with grounding techniques. According to the MIND mental health charity, panic attacks manifest as an extreme anxiety response with rapidly developing physical and mental symptoms.
